design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of 37 adults with current DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (not seeking treatment; tested after a mean of 6.9 days of urine-verified abstinence) and 41 healthy controls, with school transcripts obtained retrospectively as a premorbid proxy (for the methamphetamine group, only school years before self-reported first use). A regression fitted in the controls (adult cognitive composite on childhood grade point average, parental income, age and smoking status) predicted each methamphetamine participant's expected adult score; predicted and actual scores were compared with paired t-tests, overall and in three domains. Structural MRI (cortical thickness, FreeSurfer) in 31 per group; within the methamphetamine group, shortfalls from prediction were related to thickness. From the London laboratory at UCLA.
can_establish: Whether this methamphetamine group's adult test scores were lower than predicted from their pre-use school grades and from family and demographic factors, using a model built in these controls, and whether their grades before first use were already lower than the controls'.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the shortfall (other drug use, premorbid factors that grades do not capture and early-abstinence effects are not separated, and the prediction model explains about 40% of the variance in controls); whether scores lie within population norms (scores are standardized to the controls); or whether the shortfall lasts beyond the first weeks of abstinence (single assessment).

sample.recruitment: Internet and local newspaper advertisements; participants were paid for maintaining abstinence and completing procedures; not seeking treatment. 22 of the methamphetamine group took part while living on the research ward of the UCLA General Clinical Research Center and 15 as outpatients after it closed (their battery scores did not differ); all controls were outpatients (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: SCID for DSM-IV Axis I. Excluded: neurological disease (for example stroke, head injury with loss of consciousness over 30 minutes), structural brain abnormality on MRI, systemic, cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, HIV infection, abnormal laboratory tests, psychotropic medication, current abuse or dependence on any substance other than methamphetamine, marijuana or nicotine, and current non-substance-induced Axis I disorders (one methamphetamine participant with current social phobia was kept). Current marijuana abuse or dependence: 4 in the methamphetamine group, 2 controls (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph). Schools were asked for all transcripts and standardized test scores from elementary through high school; how many recruited people were excluded because records could not be obtained is not reported (Measures/procedures › Academic records).
sample.demographics: Methamphetamine group vs controls: age 34.0 (SD 8.9) vs 33.7 (7.6); education 12.6 (1.7) vs 12.7 (1.4) years; estimated full-scale IQ (Wechsler Test of Adult Reading) 104.9 (8.4) vs 105.0 (9.7); men 25 of 37 vs 21 of 41; employed 10 of 37 vs 24 of 41 (p<0.01); cigarette smokers 34 of 37 vs 14 of 41 (p<0.01); highest parental education 12.9 (3.2) vs 13.9 (2.6) years; Caucasian 12 vs 13, African American 3 vs 8, Hispanic 14 vs 15, Asian or Pacific Islander 3 vs 3 (Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Single assessment. Usable MRI for 31 of 37 and 31 of 41 (contraindications or motion) (Measures/procedures › Structural MRI).
sample.selection_effects: Advertisement-recruited, paid, non-treatment-seeking people with dependence who could stay abstinent and had no current comorbid dependence other than marijuana or nicotine, no HIV and no current psychiatric disorder, against healthy controls screened for current Axis I disorders; both groups needed obtainable school records. The comparison is between relatively healthy people with dependence and controls healthier than the general population, although lifetime alcohol and marijuana use disorders were not rare among controls (9 of 41 each).

exposure.measurement: SCID diagnosis of current methamphetamine dependence; drug-use history from standard intake forms (self-report), including the average amount used on days of use; urine positive for methamphetamine at entry and negative for methamphetamine and other drugs on the days of testing and MRI (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures/procedures › Self-report measures).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported: 21.9 (SD 8.2) days of use in the past 30; 6.5 (6.0) years of heavy use (at least three times a week, or twice-weekly binges); 1.1 (0.8) g a day on days of use (Table 1). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Lifetime abuse or dependence, methamphetamine group vs controls: alcohol 26 vs 9, cocaine 12 vs 0, marijuana 21 vs 9, other drugs 9 vs 0 (all p<0.01); current marijuana abuse or dependence 4 vs 2; smokers 92% vs 34% (Table 1). Within the methamphetamine group, past diagnoses were not independently associated with battery scores (ps > 0.35), and the 6 with no past diagnosis scored non-significantly lower than the 31 with one (−0.84 vs −0.60, p = 0.30) (Results › Group comparisons, 1st paragraph); the authors state that effects of methamphetamine cannot be disentangled from other substance use (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Smoking status entered the prediction model.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Mean 6.9 days (SD 2.7; range 3–30), verified by urine tests, supervised on the ward for residential participants; withdrawal rated with the Amphetamine Cessation Symptom Assessment on each testing day (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures/procedures › Self-report measures).

comparison.controls: 41 healthy controls recruited through the same advertisements, tested as outpatients; urine negative for drugs except marijuana, with saliva tests confirming brief abstinence from marijuana and at least 3 days' self-reported abstinence from drugs (Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; the groups did not differ in age, sex, education, estimated IQ, ethnicity, childhood economic class, parental education and income, or the income of the areas where they went to school (Results › Group comparisons, 1st paragraph); a grade-matched subgroup (28 per group) was analysed as a check.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood grades are the premorbid proxy (methamphetamine group: years before self-reported first use only; 4.3 vs 5.2 years of grades, p > 0.10); standardized school test scores exist for a subset. Not measured: childhood attention or conduct problems, adversity, prenatal exposures, family history of substance use disorders, and any cognitive test before first use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lifetime alcohol abuse or dependence 9 of 41, marijuana abuse or dependence 9 of 41, current marijuana abuse or dependence 2; days of alcohol and of marijuana use in the past month similar to the methamphetamine group (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Battery given over two days by clinical psychology doctoral students trained by the first author, with stand-alone and embedded effort measures (all participants passed). Attention/concentration: Trail Making A, Stroop colour and word, Digit Symbol Coding, Digit Span, Continuous Performance Test, Wisconsin Card Sorting failure to maintain set, Brief Test of Attention, Spatial Capacity Delayed Response Test. Learning/memory: Selective Reminding Test, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised. Executive function: Stroop interference, Trail Making B, verbal fluency and category switching, Wisconsin Card Sorting perseverative errors, Attention Network Task, Stop Signal Task. Composite and domain scores = means of test z-scores standardized to the control group (Measures/procedures › Cognitive battery). Structural MRI at 1.5 T, FreeSurfer 5.3 cortical thickness (Measures/procedures › Structural MRI).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scores were standardized to the control group rather than to published norms, which the authors prefer so that differences between normative datasets do not add variation; the paper therefore says nothing about whether scores were in the normal range. The prediction model explained 41% of the variance of the overall composite in controls (domains 30% to 41%).
outcomes.operationalization: Deficit = actual minus predicted score, in the averaged z-score units of the control sample, where the prediction comes from the control-group regression; no impairment threshold and no classification of individuals is used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: four predicted-versus-actual comparisons (overall and three domains), two sensitivity analyses, correlations of the deficit scores with withdrawal and with three use variables, a group comparison of thickness and two thickness models, each at p<0.05; regional thickness correlations are given uncorrected in a supplement (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; 22 of the methamphetamine group were tested while living on a research ward.

analysis.effect_sizes: Childhood grade point average before first use 2.1 (SD 0.7) vs 2.5 (0.6), p = 0.016 (standardized difference about 0.6, editors' calculation from the rounded means and SDs); standardized school test percentile 48.7 (22.7) vs 58.5 (23.7), p = 0.178, in 24 and 19 (Table 1; Results › Group comparisons, 2nd paragraph). Raw battery scores lower in the methamphetamine group, p < 0.001; the group mean is not printed, but the two subgroup means (−0.84 in 6, −0.60 in 31) give about −0.64 in control units (editors' calculation). Control-group model: composite = −0.886 − 0.008 × age + 0.025 × parental income − 0.200 × smoking status + 0.404 × grade point average, R² 0.41, p < 0.001; applied to the methamphetamine group, predicted exceeded actual scores: d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001; attention d 0.69, t(36) = 4.177, p < 0.001; memory d 0.46, t(36) = 2.805, p < 0.01; executive function not lower (printed d −0.27, t(36) = −0.169, p = 0.87). These d values equal t/√37, the mean shortfall divided by the SD of the individual shortfalls (editors' check), not differences in control-SD units. With withdrawal partialled out: d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002. Standardized test scores in place of grades (24 and 19): d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, p < 0.001. Grade-matched subgroups (28 each): d 0.71, p = 0.001. Overall and attention shortfalls correlated with grams used per day (r −0.397, p = 0.045; r −0.494, p = 0.010), not with years or frequency of use; withdrawal correlated with the overall shortfall (r −0.360, p = 0.029). Cortical thickness: no group difference (about 1% and 0.55% thinner, ns); within the methamphetamine group, memory shortfall related to whole-brain thickness (F(1,29) = 4.771, p = 0.037; left r 0.34, p = 0.060; right r 0.40, p = 0.026; n = 31). Editors' calculation from the equation and the Table 1 means (with smoking coded 1 for smokers, which reproduces a control mean of 0.00): the model's predicted mean for the methamphetamine group is about −0.30, of which grades contribute about −0.16 and smoking about −0.12; against an actual mean of about −0.64, roughly half of the group's gap from the controls is attributed by the model to the predictors and half remains as the shortfall.
analysis.covariates: Prediction model: age, parental income, childhood grade point average and current smoking status, the last included although not significant in controls because most of the methamphetamine group smoked (Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 2nd paragraph). Education was deliberately left out because methamphetamine use can affect it (Methods and materials › Data analysis, 1st paragraph); smoking, which can also follow drug use, was kept.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration mentioned; the hypotheses (lower childhood grades; current performance below prediction; shortfalls related to thinner cortex) are stated in the Introduction.
analysis.selective_reporting: Group means for the battery and the domains are not printed (they are shown in figures and for subgroups only); regional thickness correlations are only in a supplement (not read); the number of participants in the correlations with amount of use is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors call the control sample modest for prediction and recommend replication (Discussion, 7th paragraph). For d 0.61 in 37 people, the 95% interval is about 0.26 to 0.96 (editors' calculation), and wider still if the uncertainty of the prediction model were included.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 37 people with methamphetamine dependence tested after about a week of abstinence, school grades before first use were lower than the controls' (grade point average 2.1 vs 2.5), and adult composite scores were lower than a control-derived model predicted from grades, parental income, age and smoking (d 0.61; attention 0.69, memory 0.46; executive function no shortfall). The shortfall was larger with more grams used per day, remained after allowing for withdrawal, and the memory shortfall went with thinner cortex; the groups did not differ in cortical thickness.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the results "support the view that chronic methamphetamine use causes a decline in cognition" and/or a failure to develop normal abilities, adding that other drug use and unidentified factors likely contribute; the limitations state that the methods did not allow a causal relationship to be shown (Discussion, 7th paragraph). Gaps: (1) the premorbid estimate is a model with R² 0.41 fitted in 41 healthy controls and including current smoking, so the unexplained shortfall can reflect anything the model leaves out that differs between people who develop dependence and healthy controls (attention or conduct problems, adversity, other drugs), not only decline; (2) testing after about a week of abstinence, with withdrawal related to the shortfall, cannot separate lasting from early-abstinence effects; (3) the paired t-tests treat each predicted score as known, ignoring the uncertainty of a model estimated in 41 people, so the p values and intervals are too optimistic; (4) lifetime alcohol, cocaine, marijuana and other drug use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group; (5) deficit means below the model's prediction, not impaired against norms. The abstract's other conclusion, an apparent premorbid weakness, is supported by the lower grades before first use.

timeline.event: Meta-analysis cited for medium methamphetamine–control differences (d −0.34 in language to −0.66 in learning)
Same laboratory: methamphetamine group means between the 16th and 55th percentiles of norms after about 6 days of abstinence, with a retested control group
Sibling study cited for inhibitory-control deficits shared by people with stimulant dependence and their siblings (ref. 6)
Dean, Hellemann, Sugar and London (2012), educational attainment is not a good proxy for cognitive function in methamphetamine dependence, a precedent for this prediction method (ref. 39); not read
Same group's review weighing animal, cross-sectional, twin, abstinence and dose evidence on methamphetamine-caused cognitive decline
Okita et al. (2017): cortical thickness compared in about 70% of this sample, no group difference (ref. 17); not read
This study: adult scores below a prediction from pre-use school grades

replication.where_it_stands: The only study read so far that estimates a premorbid starting point for adults with methamphetamine dependence; it suggests both a premorbid weakness and a shortfall beyond it, from one laboratory and an unreplicated method, with the shortfall measured in early abstinence.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest (Competing interest).
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Department of Psychiatry and Biobehavioral Sciences (Semel Institute), Brain Research Institute and Department of Molecular and Medical Pharmacology. Same laboratory as Simon et al. (2010) and the review by Dean et al. (2013), which argued that methamphetamine probably causes mild cognitive decline in at least some people; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort with cognitive testing in adolescence before any methamphetamine use (the authors mention the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study), retested after the start of regular use and after sustained abstinence, alongside peers retested at the same intervals, with other substance use recorded throughout; meanwhile, a replication of the school-record method with a larger normative sample, prediction intervals that carry the model's uncertainty, and testing after months rather than days of abstinence.

domains.note: Other substance use disorders were far more common in the methamphetamine group and are not in the model (past diagnoses were only tested as predictors within the group); premorbid factors that grades do not capture (attention, conduct, adversity) are unmeasured; the model adjusts for grades, parental income, age and smoking and explains 41% of the variance in controls.
Dependence by SCID is reliable; amounts, duration and the date of first use (which decides which school years count) are self-reported.
Advertisement-recruited, paid volunteers and healthy controls screened for current disorders; the number excluded because school records could not be obtained is not reported.
Testing after a mean of 6.9 days of abstinence, 22 of 37 on a residential ward; withdrawal was related to the shortfall.

MRI unusable in 6 of 37 and 10 of 41; standardized school test scores for only 24 and 19; the correlations with amount of use appear to rest on about 26 people (editors' calculation, reporting issue 4).
Standard tests with effort checks, but blinding of testers to group is not reported, and scores are standardized to the controls rather than to norms.
No registered plan and several tests without correction, but the hypotheses were stated in advance and all three domains are reported, including the null for executive function.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the nearest thing to a pre-use baseline that this page has, and the analysis is transparent. But the expected score comes from a model fitted in 41 healthy controls that explains about 40% of the variance and whose own uncertainty the tests ignore; the methamphetamine group differed in ways the model does not capture and had far more other substance use disorders; and testing was in the first weeks of abstinence. It may be cited for the lower pre-use school grades of this methamphetamine group and for adult scores below a grade-based prediction (overall, attention, memory), as one laboratory's estimate; not as proof of drug-caused decline, not for impairment against norms, and not for lasting effects.

key_findings.finding: 37 non-treatment-seeking adults with current methamphetamine dependence (recruited by advertisement, paid, 22 living on a research ward) and 41 healthy controls; the methamphetamine group was tested after a mean of 6.9 days of urine-verified abstinence (SD 2.7; range 3–30).
key_findings.note: The printed SD cannot be right with that range (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: The groups were similar in age (34.0 vs 33.7), education (12.6 vs 12.7 years), estimated IQ (104.9 vs 105.0), sex, ethnicity, childhood economic class and parental education and income; the methamphetamine group was more often unemployed (27 of 37 vs 17 of 41) and more often smoked (34 of 37 vs 14 of 41).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lifetime abuse or dependence, methamphetamine group vs controls: alcohol 26 vs 9, cocaine 12 vs 0, marijuana 21 vs 9, other drugs 9 vs 0 (all p<0.01); within the methamphetamine group these past diagnoses were not independently associated with battery scores (ps > 0.35).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Methods and materials › Participants, 2nd paragraph; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Grade point average from school transcripts before self-reported first use: 2.1 (SD 0.7) in the methamphetamine group vs 2.5 (0.6) in controls, p = 0.016; standardized school test percentiles 48.7 vs 58.5 (24 and 19 participants), p = 0.178. Battery scores were lower in the methamphetamine group, p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Group comparisons of demographic characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Measures/procedures › Academic records
key_findings.note: Standardized difference in grades about 0.6 (editors' calculation from the rounded means and SDs).

key_findings.finding: In controls, grades (r 0.58), parental income (r 0.31) and age (r −0.30, trend) related to the overall composite; the model with age, parental income, grade point average and smoking status explained 41% of the variance (equation: −0.886 − 0.008 × age + 0.025 × parental income − 0.200 × smoking + 0.404 × grade point average).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Applied to the methamphetamine group, predicted overall scores were higher than actual scores: d 0.61, t(36) = 3.732, p = 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend
key_findings.note: d equals t/√37, a paired standardized difference (editors' check). Model-based decomposition (editors' calculation): predicted mean about −0.30, actual about −0.64 in control units.

key_findings.finding: By domain: attention/concentration below prediction (d 0.69, t(36) = 4.177, p < 0.001), memory below prediction (d 0.46, t(36) = 2.805, p < 0.01), executive function not below prediction (printed d −0.27, t(36) = −0.169, p = 0.87); domain models in controls had R² 0.41, 0.30 and 0.38.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The printed d for executive function does not fit its t (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal correlated with the overall shortfall (r −0.360, p = 0.029); with withdrawal partialled out, the shortfall remained (d 0.54, t(36) = 3.302, p = 0.002). Withdrawal was not related to the attention or memory shortfalls.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Larger overall and attention shortfalls went with more methamphetamine used per day (r −0.397, p = 0.045; r −0.494, p = 0.010); shortfalls were unrelated to years or frequency of use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The n is not stated; both r and p pairs fit about 26 participants, not 37 (editors' calculation; reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Checks: with standardized school test scores in place of grades (24 and 19 participants), predicted exceeded actual scores (d 1.41, t(23) = 6.888, p < 0.001); in grade-matched subgroups of 28 per group, d 0.71, p = 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The grade-matched result is printed with t(36) although each subgroup had 28 people (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Cortical thickness did not differ between the groups (about 1% and 0.55% thinner in the methamphetamine group, ns; 31 per group). Within the methamphetamine group, memory shortfall related to whole-brain thickness (F(1,29) = 4.771, p = 0.037; left hemisphere r 0.34, p = 0.060; right r 0.40, p = 0.026), with no regional pattern; the attention shortfall did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cortical thickness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Scores were standardized to the control group, not to published norms.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Measures/procedures › Cognitive battery

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: the methods do not show a causal relationship; grades and the other predictors explain about 40% of the variance; the control sample is modest for prediction; replication is recommended. They also state that effects of methamphetamine cannot be disentangled from other drug use, which could make the results an underestimate (if it preceded methamphetamine) or an overestimate (if it accompanied it).

reporting_issues.issue: Abstinence at testing is given as a mean of 6.9 days (SD 2.7; range 3–30) for 37 people. A single value of 30 with that mean would by itself make the SD at least about 3.9 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods and materials › Participants, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The mean, SD or range is misprinted; most participants were clearly tested within the first one to two weeks, but the exact distribution is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: For executive function the printed d is −0.27, but t(36) = −0.169 implies about −0.03 (every other d in the paper equals t/√n); the printed p = 0.87 fits the t.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Executive scores were essentially as predicted, not slightly better; cite as no shortfall.

reporting_issues.issue: The grade-matched subgroup analysis (28 per group) is reported with t(36); its d of 0.71 equals 3.776/√28, which fits 28 participants (27 degrees of freedom).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A degrees-of-freedom misprint; the result is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants in the correlations with grams used per day is not stated: r −0.397 with p 0.045 and r −0.494 with p 0.010 both fit about 26 participants, while the withdrawal correlation (r −0.360, p 0.029) fits 37 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predictive modeling of cognition, 4th and 5th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount-of-use association appears to rest on about 26 of 37 people, with the missing data undescribed; it should be cited as such.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's ethnicity counts sum to 39 of 41 controls and 32 of 37 in the methamphetamine group; the Other row is empty.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 2 and 5 participants are unaccounted for in the ethnicity rows.
